subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 6-year-old boy from the Mediterranean region has chronic microcytic anemia with hemoglobin 7.9 g/dL, target cells and basophilic stippling on the smear, elevated hemoglobin A2 and hemoglobin F, and normal iron studies. Sequencing shows a mutation in the TATA box of the beta-globin gene promoter that reduces binding of RNA polymerase II and its associated transcription factors.
question: Which of the following is the most direct consequence of this mutation?

options.text: Retention of an intron in beta-globin mRNA
A premature stop codon in the beta-globin coding region
Decreased efficiency of translation initiation at the Kozak sequence
Inability to add the 5-prime methylguanosine cap
A reduced rate of beta-globin gene transcription

explanation_correct: The TATA box is part of the promoter, the site where RNA polymerase II and multiple transcription factors bind upstream of the gene and increase initiation of transcription. A promoter mutation weakens this binding, so less beta-globin mRNA and protein are produced, causing beta-plus thalassemia with elevated hemoglobin A2 and F.

explanation_incorrect.A: Intron retention results from splice-site mutations, not from a promoter mutation.
explanation_incorrect.B: A premature stop codon is a nonsense mutation within the coding sequence, whereas this mutation lies in the promoter.
explanation_incorrect.C: The Kozak sequence governs translation initiation; this promoter mutation acts earlier, at transcription.
explanation_incorrect.D: Capping occurs shortly after transcription begins and is not prevented by a TATA box mutation.

educationalObjective: Promoter mutations such as those in the TATA box decrease binding of RNA polymerase II and transcription factors, reducing the rate of transcription and causing beta-plus thalassemia.
